idiom_name: tokio::task::JoinSet + join_next in a select! against tokio::time::sleep
implementation_notes: std has no runtime and no futures, so the pattern is realized through tokio: a JoinSet holds the fan-out (spawn one task per recipient), join_next() yields replies in completion order - the streaming gather - and a select! branch on a sleep applies the budget. Dropping the JoinSet aborts every task still in it, which is the cheapest reaping policy available in any language on this list; JoinSet::shutdown/abort_all make it explicit. JoinSet::join_all is the wait-for-all form, and tokio::time::timeout wraps a single future (for example a whole FuturesUnordered) when the deadline belongs around the aggregate rather than around each join.
pitfalls: Dropping a JoinSet aborts all of its tasks: a set that goes out of scope mid-gather silently kills replies that were about to arrive.
tokio::time::timeout polls the future before it checks the deadline, so a future that never yields can overshoot the budget without reporting Elapsed; CPU-bound work belongs in spawn_blocking.
Spawned tasks must be 'static: the client and the recipient data have to be owned (or Arc-shared/Clone) inside the async block.

variants.name: futures::join_all / FuturesUnordered (runtime-agnostic)
variants.idiom_name: futures::future::join_all for wait-for-all; FuturesUnordered for completion order
variants.implementation_notes: The futures crate provides the combinators without depending on tokio: join_all drives every future to completion and returns all results in input order (the wait-for-all gather; it switches internally to the more powerful FuturesOrdered for large inputs to avoid quadratic polling), while FuturesUnordered yields results as they finish for a first-answer policy. The deadline then comes from whatever timer the chosen runtime offers (tokio::time, async-io, futures-timer) wrapped around the aggregate. Choose this variant for library crates that must not force a runtime on their users; note that join_all itself imposes no budget, so a straggler blocks the gather.
pitfalls: join_all waits for every future and has no deadline of its own: the budget has to wrap the whole aggregate (or each call), otherwise one straggler defines the latency.
FuturesUnordered only makes progress while it is being polled; forgetting the driving loop (or a StreamExt combinator) makes the gather appear to finish early.
Results of join_all keep input order, not completion order, so 'how late did each reply arrive' must be measured separately if the merge needs it.

variants.name: rayon parallel iterator (CPU-bound scatter)
variants.idiom_name: par_iter().map(...).collect() + an associative reduce for the aggregate
variants.implementation_notes: When 'ask many' means shards of local computation rather than remote calls, rayon's parallel iterators are the scatter-gather: par_iter().map(...).collect() fans the work across the work-stealing pool and gathers results in the original order, while reduce/fold expresses the aggregation as an associative operation. There is no per-item deadline - a computation cannot be abandoned - so this variant fits CPU-bound work over a partition of data (shards, chunks, rows), not request/response fan-out. Mixing it with async recipients is a smell: I/O belongs to the runtime variants, and blocking I/O inside par_iter starves the pool.
variants.code_sketch:
use rayon::prelude::*;
let per_shard: Vec<Counts> = shards.par_iter().map(|s| count(s)).collect();   // scatter + gather
let total: u64 = per_shard.par_iter().map(|c| c.total()).sum();              // associative aggregate
(total, per_shard)
pitfalls: rayon tasks are neither cancellable nor time-bounded: a hung shard hangs the gather, so local work with deadlines needs an async runtime or a supervisor thread.
Blocking I/O inside par_iter occupies pool workers and starves every other rayon user in the process.
The gather is ordered per the iterator contract, so costs are charged to the whole fan-out even when only the first result is needed (find_any/any is the early-exit primitive).
